whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the MuleSoft Integration Architect exam for?

personas.label: Senior integration consultants
personas.description: You have built Mule applications for a few years and now design whole integration solutions for clients.

personas.label: Enterprise architects
personas.description: You decide how a company's systems connect, where Mule apps run, and how they meet uptime and security needs.

personas.label: Technical leads
personas.description: You lead MuleSoft teams and need to make and defend design choices on reliability, performance and deployment.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the MuleSoft Integration Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a hard exam. Few questions ask what a feature does. Most ask which design best meets a set of needs, such as no lost messages, a response under two seconds, or data that must stay on site.
bullets: 70% to pass, per MuleSoft's training site. That is a higher bar than most Salesforce exams.
Design reasoning. Most questions turn on non-functional needs like reliability, speed, scale and security.
Whole platform scope. API-led layers, deployment options, messaging, transactions, monitoring and governance all come up.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People who have designed and run Mule apps in production do best. Before you book. Aim for 75% or more on practice tests and make sure you can explain when to use a queue, a transaction or an idempotent filter.

examFormat.heading: MuleSoft Integration Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions are scenarios. A typical one describes an integration with certain needs, for example no message may be lost and the target system is often down, and asks for the best design.
bestWayToPass: Read for the requirement: Underline words like 'guaranteed', 'real time', 'on premises' or 'thousands per second'. They point to the answer.
Know the deployment options: CloudHub 2.0, Runtime Fabric and customer-hosted runtimes, and when each fits.
Learn the reliability tools: Persistent queues, Anypoint MQ, transactions, idempotent filters, retries and dead-letter queues.
Understand API-led layers: Which logic belongs in System, Process and Experience APIs, and why.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design MuleSoft integration solutions that meet real business and technical needs: choosing deployment models, making integrations reliable and fast, and keeping them secure and governed.

keyConcepts.h2: MuleSoft Integration Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Integration Architecture Patterns
blocks.body: Start from what the integration must guarantee. **Synchronous** request and reply when a caller waits for an answer. **Asynchronous** messaging with Anypoint MQ or VM queues when the caller doesn't need to wait, or the target is slow or unreliable. **Batch** processing for large scheduled data sets, using the Batch Job scope. **Publish and subscribe** when many systems need the same event. **Scatter-gather** to call several systems at once and combine the results. Every pattern has a cost: queues add delay but protect against outages, and synchronous calls are simple but fail when the target is down.

blocks.heading: API-Led Connectivity: Three-Layer Architecture
blocks.body: API-led connectivity splits APIs into three layers. **System APIs** wrap a single back-end system, such as SAP or a database, and hide its quirks. **Process APIs** combine data from several System APIs and apply business rules, such as building a full customer view. **Experience APIs** shape data for one consumer, such as a mobile app or a partner portal. The benefit is reuse: when a new app needs customer data, it calls the existing Process API instead of building new connections. Don't add layers for their own sake. A simple one-off integration may not need all three.

blocks.heading: Security Architecture for Integrations
blocks.body: Secure APIs at the edge with **API Manager policies**: client ID enforcement, OAuth 2.0 token checks, rate limiting and IP allow lists. Use TLS for data in transit, and mutual TLS when both sides must prove who they are. Keep passwords and keys out of code by using **secure properties** that are encrypted in configuration. For sensitive data, mask or encrypt fields before logging. Use separate environments and business groups so teams only reach what they own.

blocks.heading: High Availability, Resilience, and SLAs
blocks.body: For uptime, run more than one worker or replica so one failure doesn't stop the service. On customer-hosted runtimes, **clustering** shares work and state across nodes, and some tasks run on the primary node only. For no lost messages, use persistent queues, Anypoint MQ or **XA transactions** where several resources must succeed or fail together. Use **idempotent** designs, such as the Idempotent Message Validator with an Object Store, so retries don't create duplicates. **Until Successful** handles retries, and failed messages should land in a **dead-letter queue** for review. Set SLA tiers in API Manager to limit how much each consumer can call.

blocks.heading: Anypoint Governance and Centre for Enablement
blocks.body: A **Centre for Enablement (C4E)** is a small central team that helps other teams build and reuse APIs. It sets standards, publishes templates and shared assets in **Anypoint Exchange**, and measures reuse. It is not a gatekeeper that builds everything itself. **API Governance** checks API specs against rules, such as naming and security, before they are published. **Anypoint Monitoring** gives dashboards, alerts and log search across apps. Good governance means teams move faster because they start from proven assets.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the MuleSoft Integration Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions give you one or two firm requirements and several designs that almost work. Find the requirement that rules out the wrong ones.

blocks.heading: API-Led Connectivity Layers
blocks.body: One back-end system: System API. Business rules across systems: Process API. Shaping data for a channel: Experience API.

blocks.heading: Center for Enablement (C4E)
blocks.body: C4E enables and shares. If an answer says the C4E should build every API itself, it is probably wrong.

blocks.heading: API Governance Framework
blocks.body: Policies in API Manager, rules in API Governance, shared assets in Exchange and alerts in Anypoint Monitoring.

blocks.heading: Architecture Decision Trade-offs
blocks.body: Guaranteed delivery points to queues or transactions. Low latency points to synchronous calls and caching. Huge volume points to batch.

blocks.heading: Anypoint Platform Architecture
blocks.body: CloudHub 2.0 for fully managed cloud. Runtime Fabric when you need your own Kubernetes or on-premises control. Customer-hosted for full control.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After MuleSoft Integration Architect, many people add Salesforce architect credentials:

sampleQuestions.question: Orders must never be lost, even when the target ERP is down for an hour. What design fits best?
options: Store orders in memory until the ERP comes back
Queue the orders and process them when the ERP returns
Call the ERP synchronously and return an error if it is down
Drop orders that fail and ask customers to try again
sampleQuestions.explanation: A persistent queue holds each order safely until the ERP can take it, so nothing is lost during the outage.
whyWrong: Memory is lost if the app restarts.
A synchronous call fails while the ERP is down, and the order may be lost.
Dropping orders breaks the requirement.

sampleQuestions.question: Customer data from SAP, Salesforce and a billing system must be combined into one view for several apps. Where should the combining logic live?
options: In an Experience API for each app
In a Process API
In the SAP System API
In each consuming app
sampleQuestions.explanation: Process APIs combine data from several System APIs and apply business rules, so every app can reuse the same logic.
whyWrong: Experience APIs shape data for a channel. Combining it there means repeating it per app.
A System API should wrap one system only.
Putting it in each app duplicates the work.

sampleQuestions.question: A retry sends the same payment message twice. The target must not charge the customer twice. What should be used?
options: A considerably bigger CloudHub worker size
A larger timeout
An idempotent validator on an Object Store
A scatter-gather
sampleQuestions.explanation: The idempotent validator remembers message IDs it has seen and rejects repeats, so the payment only happens once.
whyWrong: More capacity doesn't affect duplicate handling.
A longer timeout doesn't stop duplicates.
Scatter-gather calls several targets at once. It doesn't stop duplicates.

sampleQuestions.question: A bank must run Mule apps on its own Kubernetes clusters inside its data centre, with central management from Anypoint Platform. Which option fits?
options: Anypoint Studio with a manual deployment
Runtime Fabric
CloudHub 2.0
A single customer-hosted runtime with no management
sampleQuestions.explanation: Runtime Fabric runs Mule apps on the customer's own infrastructure while still being managed from Anypoint Platform.
whyWrong: Studio is a design tool, not a runtime.
CloudHub 2.0 runs in MuleSoft's cloud, not the bank's data centre.
An unmanaged runtime loses central management and is harder to scale.

sampleQuestions.question: A database update and a message to a JMS queue must both succeed or both be rolled back. What should be used?
options: A batch job
An Until Successful scope only
An XA transaction across both
Two separate flows
sampleQuestions.explanation: An XA transaction ties both resources together, so either both commit or both roll back.
whyWrong: Batch jobs are for large data sets, not two-part commits.
Until Successful retries but doesn't roll back the other resource.
Separate flows can leave one done and the other not.

sampleQuestions.question: A partner is calling an API so often that other consumers are slowed down. What should the architect apply?
options: Removing the partner's access entirely
Moving the API to a batch job
A rate-limiting policy in API Manager
A bigger CloudHub worker for everyone
sampleQuestions.explanation: SLA tiers and rate limits cap how much each consumer can call, protecting the API for others.
whyWrong: Removing access isn't needed when limits will do.
A batch job doesn't serve live API calls.
More capacity treats the symptom and costs more.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main job of a Centre for Enablement (C4E)?
options: To help teams reuse APIs through shared standards
To replace the security team
To approve every code change by hand
To build every single API on behalf of the whole company
sampleQuestions.explanation: A C4E enables other teams with shared assets and guidance, so delivery speeds up and reuse grows.
whyWrong: Security still needs its own experts.
Manual approval of every change slows teams down.
Building everything centrally creates a bottleneck.

sampleQuestions.question: An app must call three systems at the same time and combine the answers before replying. Which scope fits?
options: Scatter-gather
Choice router
Until Successful
Batch Job
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scatter-gather sends requests in parallel and gathers the results into one response.
whyWrong: Choice routes to one path, not several at once.
Until Successful retries one step, it doesn't call in parallel.
Batch is for large scheduled data sets.

sampleQuestions.question: 10 million records must be moved from a database to a data warehouse every night. What is the best approach?
options: A synchronous API call per record from the warehouse
Manual export and import
A Batch Job that processes records in blocks
A single flow that loads all records into memory
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Batch Job scope splits large data sets into blocks, handles errors per record and can run in parallel.
whyWrong: Per-record API calls would be very slow.
Manual work at this scale isn't reliable.
Loading 10 million records into memory will fail.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should passwords and API keys used by a Mule app be stored?
options: Hard-coded in the flow XML
In a plain-text properties file in source control
In the API description in Exchange
In encrypted secure properties
sampleQuestions.explanation: Secure properties keep secrets encrypted in configuration, so they aren't readable in code or source control.
whyWrong: Hard-coded secrets can be read by anyone with the code.
Plain-text files in Git expose the secrets.
Exchange is for sharing APIs, not storing secrets.

sampleQuestions.question: A Mule app on customer-hosted runtimes must keep running if one server fails, and a scheduled task must run only once across all servers. What should be used?
options: A cluster, with the scheduler running on the primary node
A single server with more memory
Separate copies of the application with no link at all between them
Running the scheduler on every server
sampleQuestions.explanation: A cluster keeps the app running when a node fails, and by default schedulers run only on the primary node, so the task runs once.
whyWrong: One server is a single point of failure.
Unlinked copies would each run the task, causing duplicates.
Running on every server makes the task run several times.

sampleQuestions.question: A new mobile app needs order data shaped for small screens. Existing System and Process APIs already provide order data. What should be built?
options: A new System API to the ERP
A copy of the Process API
Direct access to the database from the mobile app
An Experience API for the mobile app
sampleQuestions.explanation: An Experience API shapes existing data for one channel. It reuses the Process API instead of building new connections.
whyWrong: A new System API duplicates an existing connection.
Copying the Process API duplicates logic.
Direct database access skips security and reuse.

sampleQuestions.question: Messages that keep failing after all retries must not block the queue and must be reviewed later. What should be used?
options: Retrying forever
Deleting the failed messages
Raising the queue's size
A dead-letter queue
sampleQuestions.explanation: A dead-letter queue moves messages that still fail out of the way, so others keep flowing and someone can review them.
whyWrong: Endless retries block the queue and waste resources.
Deleting messages loses data.
A bigger queue doesn't fix the stuck messages.

sampleQuestions.question: An API must only be called by known applications that send a valid client ID and secret. What should be applied?
options: A caching policy
A client ID enforcement
A bigger worker
An IP allow list on the API gateway
sampleQuestions.explanation: Client ID enforcement checks that each call comes from a registered application with valid credentials.
whyWrong: Caching affects speed, not security.
Worker size doesn't control access.
IP lists check where calls come from, not which application is calling.

sampleQuestions.question: A team wants to be told when an API's error rate rises above 5%. What should they use?
options: Alerts in Anypoint Monitoring
A weekly report from the C4E
Reading logs by hand each morning
Exchange ratings
sampleQuestions.explanation: Anypoint Monitoring can track error rates and send alerts as soon as a threshold is crossed.
whyWrong: A weekly report is far too late for live problems.
Reading logs by hand is slow and easy to miss.
Exchange ratings are about asset quality, not live errors.
